input.cmd:
gh issue create --title "Bug: orchestration follow-up prompt is not reliably inserted for inherited child agents" --body $'## Problem

When using orchestration agents with `inheritParentContext: true`, a follow-up prompt can fail to appear as a new instruction in the child agent. In the observed workflow, we attempted to redirect/continue an orchestrated child, but the new prompt did not get inserted into the child session.

This is especially dangerous for inherited children: the child starts from a duplicated parent transcript, so without an explicit inserted handoff/follow-up prompt it may continue interpreting the inherited conversation as if it is still the parent/orchestrator. That breaks role separation and makes parallel orchestration unreliable.

## Why this matters

The existing bootstrap wrapper in `src/mcp/shared/orchestrationPrompt.ts` is the right idea: provider-visible text is the only reliable cross-provider instruction channel. The child must see, in its own transcript/composer input, that inherited history is read-only background and that the newly supplied task is its active instruction.

If `orchestration_send_prompt` reports success but the prompt is not actually inserted/submitted, the parent believes the child was redirected while the child keeps operating from stale inherited context.

## Suspected areas

- `src/mcp/runtime/createBuiltInMcpServer.ts` around `orchestration_send_prompt`
- `submitPrompt(...)` behavior for Claude/Codex sessions
- `OrchestrationBridge.notePromptSubmitted(...)` and lifecycle reporting after prompt delivery
- `markBootstrapPromptDelivered(...)` ordering and whether bootstrap delivery is marked before/after real insertion succeeds
- renderer/session readiness path used by orchestration prompt submission

## Expected behavior

- `orchestration_send_prompt` should only return `ok: true` after the prompt has been inserted/submitted to the target child session.
- For inherited children whose bootstrap handoff has not been delivered, the first prompt must be wrapped with `buildOrchestrationBootstrapPrompt(...)`.
- If insertion/submission fails, the MCP tool must return a clear failure with a stable error code and message.
- Prompt delivery metadata should not advance in a way that makes `wait_agents` or status surfaces believe a prompt is in flight unless the prompt was actually accepted by the target session.
- The child transcript/feed should contain the inserted prompt so the child understands it is an orchestrated child, not the original parent from the inherited transcript.

## Acceptance criteria

- Add a regression test or harness coverage for `orchestration_send_prompt` against an inherited child.
- Prove the first follow-up prompt to an inherited child is wrapped and inserted exactly once.
- Prove a failed prompt insertion returns `ok: false` and does not mark bootstrap delivery or prompt submission state.
- Prove a successful prompt insertion updates lifecycle/status so the parent can wait on the child without seeing stale completion.
- Include a WHY comment near the delivery/order check explaining that inherited children can otherwise misidentify themselves as the parent agent.

## Related context

This is separate from Root Access MCP (#242). Root Access is about global/non-descendant control. This bug is about scoped orchestration prompt delivery to a valid child session and the correctness of inherited-context role handoff.
'

{"cmd":"gh issue create --title "Coordinate parallel orchestration agents in one shared worktree" --body-file - <<'EOF'
# Coordinate parallel orchestration agents in one shared worktree

## Problem

We want to launch multiple orchestration-created agents that all inherit the parent context and intentionally work in the same checkout, branch, and worktree. That is a valid workflow when the work is split by domain ownership, but the app currently treats orchestration mostly as agent lifecycle and transcript coordination. It does not make shared-worktree editing rules explicit enough for safe parallel implementation.

Today, a parent can create child agents with the same `cwd`, and those agents can independently edit files and run git commands. The missing piece is coordination metadata and guardrails around:

- declared file/domain ownership
- expected commit prefix or commit scope
- detecting overlapping dirty files before an agent edits or commits
- avoiding concurrent use of the shared git index
- reporting which child owns which chunk of a parent plan
- making collisions visible to the parent before work is lost or commits become tangled

This is separate from Root Access MCP (#242). Root Access is about explicit elevated control over non-descendant panes. This issue is about normal child orchestration where all children are owned by the same parent, but intentionally operate in one shared worktree.

## Why this matters

The consistency-audit workflow has a large checklist split by repo domains. Running five agents in separate worktrees would avoid most conflicts, but it would also fragment the branch and add merge overhead. Running five agents in the same worktree is reasonable if each agent sticks to a domain, but Agent Code should make the coordination contract visible and auditable instead of relying only on prompt instructions.

Without explicit support, the failure modes are subtle:

- two agents edit the same file after reading stale state
- one agent commits another agent's uncommitted changes
- an agent formats or typechecks a broader area and accidentally changes files outside its domain
- the parent cannot see ownership or commit readiness without inspecting every child transcript
- checklist updates in a shared markdown file collide even when implementation files are disjoint

## Proposed shape

Add orchestration metadata and guardrails for shared-worktree runs:

- Allow `orchestration_create_agent` to accept optional coordination metadata such as:
  - `ownershipPaths` or `ownershipGlobs`
  - `commitPrefix`
  - `runRole` / `workstream`
  - `sharedWorktree: true`
- Surface that metadata in orchestration list/read outputs and Dispatch status.
- Add a lightweight dirty-file ownership check before high-risk actions such as commit, close, or parent-side aggregation.
- Consider a shared-worktree commit helper or lock so only one orchestration child uses the git index at a time.
- Add parent-visible warnings when a child has touched files outside its declared ownership.
- Treat shared checklist files specially: either require serialized checklist updates or support parent-side checklist reconciliation after child outputs.

## Acceptance criteria

- Parent can launch multiple orchestration children into the same `cwd` with visible ownership metadata.
- Orchestration status/list output shows each child role, owned paths, and intended commit prefix.
- There is a clear warning when two live orchestration children have overlapping touched files.
- A child cannot accidentally commit unrelated dirty files from another child without at least a visible warning or explicit override.
- Shared-worktree orchestration has documented guidance for checklist files, commit sequencing, and verification ownership.

- one agent commits another agent's uncommitted changes

- Add a lightweight dirty-file ownership check before high-risk actions such as commit, close, or parent-side aggregation.
- Consider a shared-worktree commit helper or lock so only one orchestration child uses the git index at a time.
- Add parent-visible warnings when a child has touched files outside its declared ownership.

semanticHistory.text:
Created the GitHub issue:

https://github.com/Juliusolsson05/agent-code/issues/253

Title: `Bug: orchestration follow-up prompt is not reliably inserted for inherited child agents`

I scoped it specifically to the bug you described: with `inheritParentContext: true`, the child can see the inherited parent transcript and may think it is still the parent unless the new prompt is actually inserted into its own session. The issue separates this from Root Access (#242) and calls out the important acceptance criteria: wrapped first prompt, reliable insertion, failure reporting, no false prompt-delivery state, and a regression test/harness.
